thread.title: Why The S&P 500 Will Fall Another 20% In 2019

author: Real Finance
title: Why The S&P 500 Will Fall Another 20% In 2019
text:
Watch video below on S&P 500 price target for 2019 & why 20% downside is possible.
Is Wall Street too bullish on the S&P 500 for 2019? Wall Street Research Analysts forecast that the S&P 500 ( SPY ) will hit a target of $3,000 by end of 2019. The median earnings per share is about $172. However, studies have shown that analysts are often too bullish and are not proactive in shifting price targets. Rather, the analysts are reactive to downgrading price targets only after a significance downside event happens. A good example of this would be Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), where the majority of analysts had a "buy" rating and pump-like price targets.
My S&P 500 projected price target for 2019 S&P 500 projected to earn $174 for 2019 year. But in recession, corporate earnings fall 10-20%. This would imply S&P earnings to be $148 (assume 15% decline).
Now apply a 12 times multiple and you get $1,775. To be fair, you can apply a 14 times multiple and you get $2,070. Currently, S&P trades at 14.4 times multiple, but likely to be lowered in recession. Please see below reasons for headwinds and issues that are already playing out in the economy.
Federal Reserve will be a headwind for S&P 500 Below graph shows that once the Federal Reserve started to reduce their balance sheet in January 2018, the equity market began to experience downside. Furthermore, in October 2018, the Federal Reserve started to roll off $50 billion per month in bonds from their balance sheet. This reduction has led to draining liquidity in the U.S. economy, and U.S. stocks are a victim of this. Since the peak in January 2018, the world stock market has seen $18.3 trillion in market cap wiped off! To put even more pressure, the European Central Bank ended their quantitative easing program at the end of 2018. The Bank of Japan is still undergoing quantitative easing but has lowered asset purchases.
Quantitative easing was supportive for markets on way up. In fact, the S&P 500 rose more than what monetary experts were expecting. A good example of this would be when QE 3 occurred around 2013. During 2016, the S&P 500 was showing signs of weakness as well evidenced in the larger global economy. As a result, the ECB and Bank of Japan decided to buy even more assets ($5 trillion total) to keep the economy afloat. Therefore, it can only be assumed that quantitative tightening will deflate the bubble that we have experienced. This is an experiment that is happening in real time, and no one can accurately predict where this will end up.
Global economy slowing down? As shown in below graph, there is a fine correlation between global PMI and world stocks. Global PMI is currently around 51, which still means expansion. However, this has fallen from the peak of 54 in Q1 2018. A good example is China's PMI was reported to fall to 49 last week, which means contraction. Since China is the second largest economy, this bodes bad news for other countries, especially the U.S. Earlier this week, the U.S.'s ISM number was reported to be 54, which is still expansion, but has fallen from the recent high of 59 (in November). As the U.S. economy begins to cool off, this will continue to be reflected in the S&P 500 performance.
U.S. Home Sales - Not enough attention paid here Media outlets are not focused enough on the falling home sales. This area is a sign of confidence in the economy. People simply are not buying homes, and this is resulting in falling home prices. As home prices fall, people will begin to lose confidence in the overall economy, as most of their net worth is tied to their home. Furthermore, home sales are often a leading indicator as this shows demand for high-cost purchases. As home sales slow down, then it is likely that construction companies will also tumble. All U.S. citizens ( DIA ) ( QQQ ) will be affected by the decline.
